Dream Journey Collection
· Instructions to Zhou Yangru

[Transformation of consciousness into wisdom] To transform the eight defiled consciousnesses of ordinary beings into the four wisdoms of the Buddha — that is, to transform the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the seventh consciousness (manas) into the Wisdom of Equality, the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) into the Wonderful Observing Wisdom, and the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done.
[With outflows (sāsrava)]

Outflow is another name for affliction, and “with outflows” means possessed of affliction. The word “outflow” carries two meanings: leaking and falling. The afflictions of greed, hatred, and so forth, which day and night leak and stream forth ceaselessly through the gates of the six sense faculties, are called outflows; again, because afflictions cause a person to fall into the three evil destinies, they are likewise called outflows. Therefore, all dharmas possessed of affliction are called dharmas with outflows, and all the conditioned dharmas of the world are defiled dharmas with outflows.

“Master Zhou asked about the essential purport of the Faxiang school. The old man therefore cited the Sixth Patriarch’s Verse on Consciousness and Wisdom: ‘The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is by nature pure; the Wisdom of Equality bears a mind free from disease; the Wonderful Observing Wisdom sees, serene and sure; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done mirrors, tranquil, at its ease. Five, eight, six, seven turn in cause and fruit; they turn but names — no real essence there. If at the turning point you linger not, amid all busy stir you rest in the nāga-samādhi’s air.’”

Master Zhou requested instruction in the essential purport of the Faxiang school, so the old man (as Master Hanshan calls himself) cited the Sixth Patriarch’s Verse on Consciousness and Wisdom: “The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is by nature pure; the Wisdom of Equality bears a mind free from disease; the Wonderful Observing Wisdom sees, serene and sure; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done mirrors, tranquil, at its ease. Five, eight, six, seven turn in cause and fruit; they turn but names — no real essence there. If at the turning point you linger not, amid all busy stir you rest in the nāga-samādhi’s air.”

[Master Zhou] “Zi” (Master) was an honorific term for a person in ancient times. [Faxiang school] One of the eight schools of Mahāyāna. Because it exhaustively clarifies the nature and characteristics of all dharmas, it is called the Faxiang (“Dharma Characteristics”) school. And because it relies on the treatises on consciousness-only to illuminate the principle that all dharmas are nothing but consciousness, it is also called the Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavāda) school. [Eight schools] The Vinaya school, the Huayan school, the Tiantai school, the Three Treatise school (the Dharma-nature school), the Faxiang school (the Consciousness-Only school), the Mantra school, the Chan school, and the Pure Land school.
To make Master Hanshan’s teaching below easier to understand, let me first explain the Verse on Consciousness and Wisdom given by the Sixth Patriarch in the Platform Sutra.

“The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is by nature pure; the Wisdom of Equality bears a mind free from disease; the Wonderful Observing Wisdom sees, serene and sure; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done mirrors, tranquil, at its ease.”

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom — its nature is pure. The Wisdom of Equality — the mind is free from disease. The Wonderful Observing Wisdom — seeing and hearing carry no contrivance. The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done — it is like the round mirror.

[The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is by nature pure] The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is transformed into. The ālayavijñāna contains numberless seeds of karma and exerts a defiling influence on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Now, when consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it defiles no more; hence it is said to be “pure by nature.” [The Wisdom of Equality bears a mind free from disease] The Wisdom of Equality is what the seventh consciousness (manas) is transformed into. The principal function of the manas is deliberation and calculation, and this is the great illness that produces birth and death. Now, when consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it no longer deliberates or calculates; hence it is said that “the mind is free from disease.” [The Wonderful Observing Wisdom sees without contrivance] The Wonderful Observing Wisdom is what the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) is transformed into. The principal function of the sixth consciousness is to discriminate when the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) come into contact with the corresponding five sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch). Now, when consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it merely observes and no longer discriminates; hence it is said that “seeing carries no contrivance” (that is, even in seeing there is no effort of discrimination). [The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done mirrors like the round mirror] The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done is what the first five consciousnesses are transformed into; once transformed into wisdom, it merely reflects the objects before it without discriminating, hence it is said to “mirror like the round mirror.”
“Five, eight, six, seven turn in cause and fruit; they use but names — no real essence there. If at the turning point you linger not, amid all busy stir you rest in the nāga-samādhi’s air.”

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses are transformed on the causal ground, while the first five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are accomplished naturally on the fruition ground (at the moment of Buddhahood). This transformation (of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms) only changes their names and appearances (their states), while their substance is not twofold (it has no real essence). If, at the point where the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom, one does not linger — if one turns decisively and resolutely (this is where one does the work in daily life) — then even in the bustling red dust of the world one is like a dragon lying hidden in the deep, dormant and still, ever abiding in the dragon’s samādhi.

[Fruition ground] As opposed to the “causal ground,” it is the stage of attainment reached through cultivation on the causal ground. Here “fruition ground” refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. [Profuse activity] Arising in great abundance; here it refers to the teeming profusion of the myriad phenomena. [Nāga-samādhi] “Nāga” is translated as “dragon.” The “nāga-samādhi” is the “dragon’s samādhi,” like a dragon lying hidden in the deep, dormant and still. [If at the turning point you linger not] To turn without the slightest hesitation, like cutting off a finger the instant a venomous snake bites it. [Amid all busy stir you rest in the nāga-samādhi’s air] Although one stands in the bustling red dust of the world amid the teeming profusion of phenomena, one ever abides in the dragon’s samādhi.
The main text continues below:

“These eight lines fully express the innermost essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and lay bare the very root of nature and characteristics. Yet those who count others’ treasure and reckon grains of sand, greedy for more than they can chew, generally regard this as idle furniture and have never looked upon it with a proper eye — which is most pitiable indeed.”

These eight lines of the Verse on Consciousness and Wisdom fully express the innermost essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and lay bare the very root of nature and characteristics. Those who merely circle around in names and terminology without genuine cultivation (the sort who count others’ treasure and reckon grains of sand), greedy for more than they can chew (not knowing the true flavor within), all regard this as idle furniture and have never looked at it closely with a proper eye — truly pitiable.

[Counting treasure] Counting the treasure of others — referring to those who, without genuine practice in accordance with the teachings, merely show off with words. [Reckoning sand] Going into the sea not to gather treasure but to count grains of sand — referring to those who sink into names and terminology instead of realizing the Way through actual practice.

“They all say that the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate and did not understand the teachings — how then could he have said such a thing? Little do they know that the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is summed up completely in just eight words: ‘The three realms are only mind; the ten thousand dharmas are only consciousness.’ Because everything is only mind, the three realms are still and silent, utterly without a single thing; because everything is only consciousness, the ten thousand dharmas stand in their teeming profusion. For the ten thousand dharmas are merely manifested from consciousness; seek them in one’s own mind, and their essence (self-nature) cannot be found at all. Therefore the Buddhas and Patriarchs taught people only to say that not a shred of anything can be obtained outside the mind — which is precisely the ‘fundamentally not a single thing’ that came forth at Huangmei in the dead of night. In this one phrase are contained all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods and all the Patriarchs of successive generations, and it cannot be broken through; therefore the robe and bowl were settled upon him. Even the two branches and the five houses all derive from this one phrase — how could there ever have been a division between the nature school and the characteristics school?”

They suppose that the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate and did not understand the scriptures and teachings — how then could he possibly reveal the root of nature and characteristics? Little do they know that the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is summed up completely in just eight words: “The three realms are only mind; the ten thousand dharmas are only consciousness.” Because everything is only mind, the three realms are still and silent, utterly without a single thing; because everything is only consciousness, the ten thousand dharmas stand in their teeming profusion, a forest of myriad phenomena. Since the ten thousand dharmas are all manifested from consciousness, seek them in one’s own mind, and their essence (self-nature) cannot be found at all. Therefore what the Buddha and the Patriarchs taught people amounts to no more than saying that not a shred of anything can be obtained outside the mind — which is precisely Huineng’s “fundamentally not a single thing.” In this one phrase are contained all that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods and the Patriarchs of successive generations have said; it is a truth that cannot be overturned, and for this reason the Fifth Patriarch transmitted the robe and bowl to him. Even the two branches and the five houses are all derived from this one phrase — how could there ever have been a division between the nature school and the characteristics school?
[For the ten thousand dharmas are merely manifested from consciousness] In the Dream Journey Collection
The Veritable Record of Master Hanshan’s Autobiographical Chronicle states:

‘Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Relying on consciousness, one is defiled; relying on wisdom, one is pure. In defilement there is birth and death; in purity there are no Buddhas.’

[“Fundamentally not a single thing” came forth at Huangmei in the dead of night] When Huineng uttered “fundamentally not a single thing,” this essential purport of the Buddha-dharma, the Fifth Patriarch therefore transmitted the patriarchal seat to him in the dead of night. Hence it is said: on Mount Huangmei, in the dead of night, there suddenly emerged a Patriarch of “fundamentally not a single thing.” [Huangmei] Mount Huangmei, where the East Chan Monastery of Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of the Chan school, was located. [Two branches] Below the Fifth Patriarch there were two branches: the Northern school of Shenxiu and the Southern school of Huineng. The watershed between these two branches is whether one has awakened to the truth of “fundamentally not a single thing.” [Five houses] Below the Sixth Patriarch there were five houses (also called the five families): the Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan houses. [Nature school and characteristics school] That is, the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-characteristics school. 1. The Dharma-nature school (the Three Treatise school among the eight schools), briefly called the nature school: it demolishes the characteristics of the ten thousand dharmas and reveals the true empty and quiescent nature of all dharmas. 2. The Dharma-characteristics school (the Consciousness-Only school), briefly called the characteristics school: it attributes the arising of the ten thousand dharmas to the ālayavijñāna, takes the ālayavijñāna as the root of all defiled and pure causes and effects, and, with regard to the dharmas it produces, broadly distinguishes their names and meanings — hence it is called the Dharma-characteristics school.

“Now, examining the Verse on Consciousness and Wisdom, I offer a brief annotation. If we take ‘the three realms are only mind,’ then there is no place to begin. Because when one is deluded about this mind it changes and becomes consciousness; then it loses the name ‘suchness’ and is called only the ālayavijñāna, also called the storehouse consciousness. This consciousness is what the entire suchness has been transformed into. This is precisely what is called ‘the coming together of the born-and-perishing with the unborn-and-imperishable’ — the root of truth and falsity, delusion and awakening, and the basis of birth and death, of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: ‘The storehouse-consciousness sea is ever-abiding; stirred by the wind of sense-objects, mighty waves surge in the dark abyss, without a moment’s cessation.’ Since it says that the storehouse consciousness is the ālayavijñāna, and yet says it is ever-abiding, then it is fundamentally unmoving. What moves, then, is not the storehouse consciousness but only the wind of sense-objects.”

Now I use the Verse on Consciousness and Wisdom to illuminate the principle of “the three realms are only mind; the ten thousand dharmas are only consciousness.” If we take “the three realms are only mind” (all that exists in the three realms is nothing but one mind), then there is no place to begin. Because when one is deluded about this mind (suchness) it changes and becomes consciousness; then it loses the name “suchness” and is called only the ālayavijñāna, also called the storehouse consciousness. This consciousness is what the entire suchness has been transformed into. This is precisely what is called “the coming together of the born-and-perishing with the unborn-and-imperishable” — the root of truth and falsity, delusion and awakening, and the basis of birth and death, of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: “The storehouse-consciousness sea is ever-abiding; stirred by the wind of sense-objects, mighty waves surge in the dark abyss, without a moment’s cessation.” In the scripture, since it speaks of the storehouse consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) and yet says it is ever-abiding, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally unmoving. What moves, then, is not the storehouse consciousness but the wind of sense-objects.

“The verse says, ‘If the object before one does not exist, the mind too does not exist.’ Thus, that which grasps the sense-objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the born-and-perishing mind. This born-and-perishing mind is forcibly named the seventh consciousness, but in truth it is the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness — what is called the ‘living impulse.’ If this impulse ceases for a moment, the objects before one instantly become void, and even though the sixth consciousness can discriminate, there is nothing left upon which it can settle. As for the first five consciousnesses, they originally have no separate substance but are merely the storehouse consciousness’s functioning in response to conditions; they can only illumine objects and cannot discriminate, hence it is said they ‘mirror like the round mirror.’ That which discriminates the five sense-objects is not the five consciousnesses but the sixth consciousness that arises simultaneously with them; hence the sixth consciousness is said to ‘hold the merit.’ If it does not give rise to discrimination, then ‘seeing carries no contrivance.’”

The verse says: “If the object before one does not exist, the mind too does not exist.” Therefore, that which grasps the sense-objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the born-and-perishing mind. This born-and-perishing mind is forcibly named the seventh consciousness (manas), but in truth it is the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness (the storehouse consciousness) — what is called the “living impulse.” If this living impulse (the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness) ceases for a moment, the objects before one instantly become void, and even though the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) can discriminate, there is nothing left upon which it can settle (nothing left to discriminate). As for the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness), they originally have no separate substance; they are merely the storehouse consciousness’s functioning in response to conditions. These first five consciousnesses can only reflect the sense-objects and cannot discriminate, hence it is said they “mirror like the round mirror.” That which can discriminate the five sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch) is not the first five consciousnesses but the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) that arises simultaneously with them; hence the sixth consciousness is said to “hold the merit.” If it (the sixth consciousness) does not give rise to discrimination, then “seeing carries no contrivance.”

[If this impulse ceases] If this living impulse (the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness) ceases. Above it was said that “in truth it is the stirring thought of the eighth consciousness, what is called the ‘living impulse.’” The “impulse” (ji) is that from which the change of things arises.

“Looking at it from this angle, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally true, hence it is said to be ‘pure by nature.’ Its fault lies in a single thought giving rise to the mind, and this is the illness of the mind. Where there is arising there is ceasing; this arising and ceasing is like the flowing of water — there is no flow apart from the water. It is only because of the water’s nature of not abiding that a flowing appearance is seen; and once there is flow, it is clear that this is not the still water of a deep pool. Therefore the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing: the arising, abiding, and ceasing of characteristics, and the arising, abiding, and ceasing of perfusion. These two kinds of arising and ceasing both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If this arising and ceasing does not cease, the first seven consciousnesses arise; if this arising and ceasing ceases, then there remains only the single essence of truth, and the nature of suchness is thereby restored. Once restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom, hence it is said that ‘the mind is free from disease.’”

Looking at it from this angle, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally true, hence it is said to be “pure by nature.” Its fault lies in a single thought giving rise to the mind, and this is the illness of the mind. Where there is arising there is ceasing; this arising and ceasing is like the flowing of water — there is no flow apart from the water. It is only because this water has a nature of not abiding that there is a flowing appearance; and once there is flow, it is clear that this is not the still water of a deep pool. Therefore the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says that the various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing: the arising, abiding, and ceasing of characteristics, and the arising, abiding, and ceasing of perfusion. These two kinds of arising and ceasing both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If this arising and ceasing does not cease, the first seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and manas consciousness) arise; if this arising and ceasing ceases, the first seven consciousnesses cease, and there remains only the storehouse consciousness, this single essence of truth, and the nature of suchness is thereby restored. Once restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom, hence it is said that “the mind is free from disease.”

“What the Sixth Patriarch, the great master, versified concerns transforming the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness is transformed into; the Wisdom of Equality is what the seventh consciousness is transformed into; the Wonderful Observing Wisdom is what the sixth consciousness is transformed into; and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done is what the first five consciousnesses are transformed into. Because delusion belongs to the functioning of the storehouse consciousness, its truth likewise shares in ‘mirroring like the round mirror.’ However, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are transformed first on the causal ground, while the five and the eighth form one body and are perfected only at the fruition. Seen in this way, the consciousnesses are fundamentally not real, and yet delusion gives them two functions; hence it is said that they ‘turn but names alone’ — the name changes while the substance does not. Moreover, this substance does not reside in dhyāna practice but only in everything of daily life. Sages and ordinary beings alike turn at this point; the difference lies only between lingering and not lingering. Hence there is the distinction between sage and ordinary being, between delusion and awakening. Master Zhou, since you aspire to this, look carefully at the turning point in daily life, and examine it — determine it — for yourself.”

The verse composed by the Sixth Patriarch, the great master, concerns transforming the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness is transformed into; the Wisdom of Equality is what the seventh consciousness (manas) is transformed into; the Wonderful Observing Wisdom is what the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) is transformed into; and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done is what the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) are transformed into. Because the first five consciousnesses are the deluded functioning of the storehouse consciousness, now that they are transformed into wisdom they, together with the wisdom transformed from the storehouse consciousness, are alike a round mirror. However, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are transformed first on the causal ground, while the first five and the eighth consciousness form one body and are transformed into wisdom only at the fruition ground (at Buddhahood). Seen in this way, the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally not real, and yet delusion gives them the two functions of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing; hence it is said that they “turn but names alone” — the name changes while the substance does not. Moreover, the transformation of this substance does not reside in dhyāna practice but only in every arising of thought and movement of mind in daily life. Ordinary beings and sages (bodhisattvas from the first stage upward) all turn at the point where thought arises and the mind moves; whether one is ultimately turning wisdom into consciousness or consciousness into wisdom depends solely on lingering or not lingering. Hence there is the distinction between sage and ordinary being, between delusion and awakening. Master Zhou, since you aspire to this, look carefully and intently at the turning point in daily life, and scrutinize it closely: is one turning in the right direction (transforming consciousness into wisdom) or in reverse (transforming wisdom into consciousness)?

[Turn but names alone, change the name but not the substance] This means that the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms are two states of one body, just as ice and water appear utterly different — hence there is the name “ice” and the name “water” — but in fact they are merely

in two states — one body, two states. When ice melts into water, the name changes, yet the substance remains

; hence it is said, “turn but names alone, change the name but not the substance.” [Sages and ordinary beings turn at the same point, the difference lying only between lingering and not lingering] The sages have awakened and do not linger on greed, hatred, and delusion, so they are transforming consciousness into wisdom; ordinary beings are deluded and have not yet relinquished their feelings toward greed, hatred, and delusion (they linger), so they do the opposite, transforming wisdom into consciousness. [Sage] From ordinary being to Buddhahood there are altogether fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wonderful enlightenment. Among these, the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences have cut off only the delusions of views and thoughts, while the delusions of numberless dust and the delusion of ignorance still remain; they are called the “worthy.” Bodhisattvas from the first ground upward, who have stilled falsity, accord with the truth, and have realized the genuine, are called “sages.”
